issues.issue: This provision says Shares are offered to "qualified institutional purchasers," while the Section 3(c)(7) provision (c075) conditions the exemption on ownership only by "qualified purchasers" and the cover page addresses "qualified institutional or accredited investors." The three eligibility standards are not the same and a court could be asked which governs.

This purpose recital promises lenders a "continuous source of managed investment for cash collateral," while the operative redemption provision (c028) lets Wells Fargo postpone payment or suspend redemptions in circumstances specified in the Declaration of Trust. A court could be asked whether the recited purpose colours the discretion in the operative term.

After naming Galliard, Peregrine and Wells Capital, the clause adds "or other direct or indirect registered investment advisory subsidiaries," leaving the reach of the general category against the named specifics uncertain. Whether an unaffiliated or non-registered adviser could be used turns on that catch-all.

"Sole discretion" is unqualified and the clause supplies no standard by which allocation among advisers could be tested. Its interaction with any implied good-faith limit is the only thing to construe.

Each Share is said to represent "an undivided proportionate interest in all assets and liabilities of the CI Term Trust," while c031 states that ownership of Shares gives Shareholders no title in or to Trust property and no right to division of it. A court could be asked to reconcile the proprietary language with the disclaimer.

Shares are offered "at the then applicable value per Share (as defined below)," but no definition of value per Share appears below; the valuation section only says assets are valued at current market value and redemptions occur at the value "as determined by Wells Fargo." The dangling cross-reference leaves the pricing term unfixed.

The minimum is "determined by Wells Fargo in the efficient management of the securities lending and investment program" — a garbled and standardless formula giving no measurable benchmark. "Efficient management" cannot be applied as a limit on the discretion.

"Then current market value" is undefined and the memorandum elsewhere permits holdings (private placements, Rule 144A, illiquid securities) for which no market price exists. How value is fixed for such assets is left open.

"All expenses incurred in connection with the acquisition, ownership and transfer of its Investments" is a general phrase followed by a parenthetical list of specifics, leaving unclear whether unlisted charges fall inside it. Ejusdem generis could cut the general words down to the enumerated kinds.

Fees may be taken "in amounts that are determined to be reasonable by the Trustee" — the reasonableness standard is committed to the very party being paid, with no benchmark. Whether "reasonable" is a substantive limit or purely self-judged is open to construction.

This provision flatly bars transfer or assignment of Shares, while the Tax Matters provision (c081) says only that Wells Fargo "intends to restrict transfers of ownership" to avoid publicly-traded-partnership status. The two cannot easily be squared on whether any transfer is possible.

Payment is due "within seven days after the redemption date" while the redemption right itself is exercisable on "seven (7) business days" notice, and the postponement/suspension right applies in unspecified "certain circumstances as specified in the Declaration of Trust." Both the day-count mismatch and the open-ended trigger give a court something to construe.

The reserved right to postpone payment or suspend redemptions sits against the stated purpose of the Trust (c003) to give securities lenders a continuous, daily-liquid source of managed investment and against the daily-liquidity investment objective (c039). A court could be asked whether the suspension power can be exercised so as to defeat those stated terms.

The exculpation is written as "no liability ... for any act or omission, provided that such act or omission does not involve bad faith, willful misconduct, negligence or reckless disregard," so the carve-out for ordinary negligence is expressed only as a negative proviso. Whether the clause exculpates simple negligence, and whose "duties to the Trust" set the standard, is genuinely contestable.

The exculpation runs to "Wells Fargo and other agents of the Trust" without reference to Wells Fargo's separate roles as Trustee and self-appointed Investment Manager (c008), and it must be read against the Declaration of Trust standards it does not restate. A court could be asked which capacity and which standard governs.

The denial of any "title in or to the property of the Trust" is hard to square with c013, which gives each Share "an undivided proportionate interest in all assets and liabilities of the CI Term Trust." The instrument read as a whole leaves the nature of the Shareholder's interest unsettled.

Indemnity is payable "from the assets of the Trust" generally, whereas c013 makes each Share an interest in the assets and liabilities of the CI Term Trust series alone. Whether one series' assets answer for another series' shareholder liability is left unresolved.

The closing words "unless expressly required under the Maryland Act" have no antecedent — nothing states what the Act might require — and the clause refers to Shares "in the Fund," a term used nowhere else in the memorandum. The amendment power's limits therefore cannot be read off the words.

The premise that "the Declaration does not confer any independent rights to Shareholders" conflicts with c030 and c031, which say Shares give "the rights provided in the Declaration of Trust," and with the redemption rights described in c028. A court could be asked whether unilateral amendment can extinguish those stated rights.

The flat statement that decisions "are made independently from those other accounts" sits awkwardly with c034's disclaimer that Wells Fargo's obligations are not exclusive and with c026's permission to trade through affiliated brokers. Whether this sentence is an enforceable undertaking or mere description could be argued.

The objective turns on "high-quality" securities and on "safety of principal and daily liquidity requirements" as the "prime considerations" — each phrase is evaluative and undefined, and "prime considerations" does not say whether they are limits or merely priorities. A dispute over whether a purchase complied would turn entirely on these words.

The stated premium on safety of principal and daily liquidity is difficult to reconcile with the policies permitting up to 15% in illiquid securities (c046), five-year maturities (c055) and mortgage- and asset-backed paper (c044). A court could be asked whether the objective constrains the permitted-investment list or is overridden by it.

"It is anticipated that the securities purchased ... may be matched in maturity and/or index" is doubly hedged, so whether any obligation to match loan maturities exists at all is unclear. "Anticipated ... may" cannot be applied as a rule.

"Will endeavor to maintain a stable $10.00 price per Share" states an undertaking in the same sentence as a disclaimer that no assurance is given, leaving the content of the endeavour obligation open. Whether this creates any duty is contestable.

The mandatory "shall comply with the following portfolio guidelines" sits against the cover-page statement that the Memorandum is only a summary "qualified in its entirety by reference to the documents themselves," and against c086's description of the document as an "overview." Whether the guidelines are binding terms at all is exactly the kind of question a court would face.

The first sentence says the Trust "may only invest in ... obligations rated in the highest short-term rating category," and the next sentence then permits unrated obligations "determined to be of comparable quality by Wells Fargo" — the restriction and the permission contradict one another within the clause. "Comparable quality," judged by the manager itself, adds a second undefined standard.

A short-term-rating-only test cannot readily be applied to the instruments the diversification list (c044) authorises — mortgage-backed, asset-backed and corporate bonds and debentures — or to the five-year maturities allowed by c055, which carry long-term rather than short-term ratings. Harmonising quality with the permitted-investment and maturity provisions leaves a genuine gap.

The list mixes narrow items with open-ended categories — "Debt obligations, including commercial paper and participations," "Units of business trusts or other private placement securities," "Variable rate or issues with put features" — so the outer boundary of what may be bought is undefined. It also authorises investment of assets of "the Fund," a term used nowhere else in the memorandum.

The breadth of the permitted list is hard to reconcile with the Portfolio Quality restriction (c043) that the Trust "may only invest" in obligations with the highest short-term rating, and with the safety-of-principal and daily-liquidity objective in c039. A court could be asked whether the list expands or is cut down by those provisions.

The exception for "repurchase agreements collateralized by the investment securities listed above" does not make clear whether "listed above" means the exceptions just enumerated or the whole permitted-investment list. The referent changes the reach of the 5% limit.

The 5% single-issuer cap is difficult to square with c062, which lets the Trustee invest "all of the assets" of the CI Term Trust in shares of another series of the same Trust. Whether the series exception in this clause covers that is not stated.

A permitted 15% allocation to illiquid securities is in tension with the investment objective in c039, under which daily liquidity is a "prime consideration." Whether the specific 15% allowance or the general objective governs is a live question.

"Will generally be considered illiquid" states a presumption without identifying who rebuts it or on what basis, and the parenthetical market test ("an active secondary market") is itself evaluative. The word "generally" leaves the rule's application indeterminate.

The 25% industry cap is followed by an exception that "the financial services or banking industry may exceed 25%" with no ceiling at all, so the exception can swallow the rule. Whether any limit constrains financial-sector concentration is unresolved on these words.

"Will review the portfolio and may consider adopting guidelines ... as it deems appropriate in its discretion" is purely precatory, giving no ascertainable obligation. What, if anything, the manager must do is not stated.

This deferral runs until six months after inception or $100 million in assets, "whichever is later," while the parallel maturity deferral (c054) uses the identical formula with "whichever is earlier." The mismatch between the two twin provisions cannot be harmonised on its face.

A 190-day maximum dollar-weighted average maturity sits against c055's five-year maximum maturity for an individual security and c052's "shortest of" deeming rules, which can make long instruments count as very short. Whether the average is a real constraint on duration is contestable.

The special rule for variable rate demand obligations overlaps the general "shortest of" rule in c052, which already covers interest-rate resets and put dates. Which rule governs an instrument answering both descriptions is not stated.

"Whichever is earlier" makes the deferral expire at six months even before any assets are invested, which reads as a slip for "later" and reverses the clause's evident sense. The mechanical choice of word decides when the 190-day limit bites.

This clause defers the maturity requirement until the six-month or $100 million trigger, "whichever is earlier," while the identically worded diversification deferral (c050) says "whichever is later." The two cannot both reflect the same intended scheme.

A five-year maximum maturity is hard to reconcile with the Portfolio Quality rule (c043) permitting only obligations with the highest short-term rating and with the daily-liquidity objective in c039. Which provision limits the other is a genuine question on the whole instrument.

"The industry convention for these types of securities will be used" imports an unidentified external standard for weighted average life, with no source named and no tie-breaker if conventions differ. The maximum maturity of a whole class of holdings turns on that undefined phrase.

The clause turns on "Unrated Security," a capitalised term defined nowhere in the memorandum, and on whether the security "presents minimal credit risks" — with the remedial step left wholly to what "the Investment Manager determines is in the best interests" of the Trust. There is no ascertainable duty to sell or hold.

Allowing a downgraded security to be retained at the manager's discretion is in tension with c043's statement that the Trust "may only invest in" obligations with the highest short-term rating. Whether the quality restriction is a continuing or purchase-time-only test is left open.

Permitting the Trustee to invest "all of the assets" of the CI Term Trust in another series is hard to square with the 5% single-issuer limit (c045), the 15% illiquid cap (c046) and the daily-liquidity objective (c039), since another series' units are private placement interests. Reading it literally would nullify the diversification guidelines.

"A leading money market index such as Fed Funds or LIBOR" pairs an open-ended general standard with two examples, leaving unclear whether other indices qualify and what makes one "leading." The permissible index set cannot be read off the words.

The credit-risk description refers to "the counterparty to a derivative," although derivatives appear nowhere in the permitted-investment list (c044) and dual index and inverse floaters are prohibited by c064. The mismatch could be used to argue the permitted universe is wider than the list suggests.

The acknowledgement that illiquid holdings may prevent sale at an advantageous time or price cuts against the investment objective in c039, which makes daily liquidity a prime consideration. A court could be asked whether the risk disclosure qualifies the objective or vice versa.

Reliance on Rule 506 of Regulation D (which turns on accredited investors) is stated alongside c075's reliance on Section 3(c)(7) (which requires "qualified purchasers") and c001's offer to "qualified institutional purchasers." The instrument gives three different investor-eligibility criteria without reconciling them.

The exemption is premised on Shares being owned only by "qualified purchasers," whereas c001 offers Shares to "qualified institutional purchasers" and the cover page addresses "qualified institutional or accredited investors." Which class of investor may in fact hold Shares is left inconsistent across the document.

The statement that no ERISA Plan investors are anticipated is difficult to square with c003, which describes the Trust's purpose as serving securities-lending clients of Wells Fargo as lending agent, a class that commonly includes ERISA plans. Whether Plan money may be invested is left unresolved.

Saying Wells Fargo merely "intends to restrict transfers of ownership" presupposes some transfers are possible, while c027 states flatly that Shares "may not be transferred or assigned." The two provisions describe different transfer regimes.

Describing the Memorandum as merely "an overview of the CI Term Trust and its policies" pulls against c042's mandatory direction that investments "shall comply with the following portfolio guidelines." Whether the guidelines are contractually binding or only descriptive is precisely what this tension raises.

The return obligation is triggered by three disjunctive events ("upon delivery of updated offering materials, upon reaching a decision not to subscribe, or if such subscription is not accepted"), none of which addresses a recipient who does subscribe and is accepted. The clause's operation in that case cannot be read off its words.
